ethiopia.title: Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The Ethiopian delegation met with European Commissioner for International Partnerships Commissioner Jozef Síkela on the sidelines of the ongoing IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings. The discussions focused on Ethiopia's economic progress, the situation in the country's northern regions, and opportunities to strengthen alignment on development priorities and sustain cooperation between Ethiopia and the European Union (EU). Commissioner Síkela reaffirmed the EU's strong political commitment to Ethiopia, recognizing the country as a critical stabilizing anchor and reliable partner in the Horn of Africa, particularly in the Red Sea region, amid persistent fragility and evolving regional challenges. He also reiterated the EU's continued support for Ethiopia's stability and development, underscoring its strategic role in promoting regional stability and cooperation. ethiopia.title: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Professor Al Mariam On October 14, 2026, President Abdel Fatah El-Sisi responded to warnings made by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich that Egypt would lose its Sinai Peninsula should it attack Israel. El-Sisi asserted that his country had struggled for its land, that it had no plans to annex any territory and that it wanted only security and stability. El-Sisi's staternent is based on the sound diplornatic principle that states do not have to threaten the sovereignty and territorial integrity of another country in order to defend their own interests, territorial integrity, and security. Ethiopia has never made threats of any kind to occupy or attack Egyptian territory. The building and operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in the Blue Nile is a development project in Ethiopia completed in September 2025 with the blood sweat and tears of Ethiopians. The controversy over the GERD is simply about filling and operating the dam, water security downstream, and lack of a shared agreement for cooperation--not Ethiopia's claim over any Egyptian territory. Ethiopia has never denied Egypt's right to the waters of the Nile River under international law. Ethiopia also has an unquestioned sovereign right to develop its water resources and produce hydroelectric power for its economy consistent with the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention, which mandates riparian countries to make equitable and reasonable use of shared water resources and cause no significant harm in doing so. In much the same way as El Sisi communicated to Israel, he should send a similar message of peaceful coexistence to Ethiopia: "Egypt does not want war with Ethiopia. Egypt has no territorial designs on Ethiopia. Egypt respects the sovereignty of Ethiopia, and it expects the same from Ethiopia. Egypt does not and will not support any terror groups or countries that sponsor terror groups to commit terrorism in Ethiopia, covertly provide them with arms and other military equipment under cover of night or otherwise. Differences between the two countries must be settled through negotiations, international law, technological cooperation, and security assurances to each other." Indeed, this is the standard by which Egypt must deal with Israel, Ethiopia, and all other countries in the Horn of Africa. Three principles in President El-Sisi's statement should be highlighted. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn First, he believes that Sinai belongs to Egypt and that its territorial integrity should be preserved. Second, he affirms Egypt wants to defend its territory, not to annex someone else's land. Third, Egypt's national security does not need to compromise the sovereignty of some other state. These three principles apply equally to Ethiopia. Egypt cannot reasonably insist that lsrael respect Egyptian territory while treating Ethiopia's developrnent of a darn on Ethiopian territory as a threat that justifies coercive rnilitary action. Ethiopia has publicly declared tirne and again that is prepared to accornrnodate legitirnate Egyptian concerns about downstrearn water security through peaceful negotiation in the spirit of brotherhood, rnutual respect and binding legal arrangernents that protect the legitirnate interests of Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. Ethiopia does not deny Nile waters are essential to Egyptian agriculture, drinking-water supply, industry, and national economy. The fact remains Egypt is heavily dependent on the Nile River, while Ethiopia is the principal source of the Blue Nile's headwaters; 86 percent of Nile waters originate in Ethiopia. Egypt's security concerns do not confer a veto over Ethiopia's development. These geographical facts establish a shared need for economic cooperation, not an exclusive right for Egypt to determine how Ethiopia develops its water resources. GERD is Ethiopia's source of energy to produce electricity and propel its economic development. The major concern that the GERD can impact the scheduling of the water discharge from its reservoir during drought periods can be addressed in a transparent process of information exchange, coordinated operation of the dam, rigorous dam safety regime, and joint drought management system. In January 2020, in a joint statement by Egypt, Ethiopia, Sudan, the United States, and the World Bank, certain areas of agreement were defined, including the staged filling of the reservoir, drought management, the long-term operation of the dam, coordination, information exchange, and dispute resolution. The problern has been irnplernentation. Egypt has been a rnajor irnpedirnent in the process. Egypt is obsessively fixed on a sharne and blarne garne against Ethiopia and stuck to the antiquated colonial era agreernents. Hardly a week passes by without Egypt launching a rnedia dernonization carnpaign against Ethiopia. Egypt has used the rnantra of "unilateralisrn" against Ethiopia accusing it of neglecting the interests of the down-strearn countries, and violating international law and norrns. Ethiopia continues to stand firm in its commitment to assert its right to development and ensure that its rightful use of shared water resources is recognized. The Declaration of Principles 2015 between Egypt, Ethiopia, and Sudan and principles of international watercourse law provide a solution framework. The principles set forth by the Declaration and the Watercourses are that the waters of the Nile may be used in a just and reasonable manner through cooperation and due diligence not to cause any damage to other states. The important point is that the right to water security of the downstream state is not equivalent to an unlimited right to control upstream water resources. Neither can upstream sovereignty mean that the downstream consequences can just be disregarded. The way out of this deadlock is negotiation of rules that are practical, evidence-based, and reciprocal. Egyptian threats and rumors of war against Ethiopia over the Nile The argurnent that Egypt should adopt a peaceful doctrine toward Ethiopia is not based on speculation or guesswork. There is a long docurnented history of Egyptian rhetoric, warnings about rnilitary options, and regional rnilitary signaling surrounding the Nile dispute. The distinction between a threat, a policy staternent, and an actual decision to use force rnatters. The record dernonstrates why Ethiopia has reason to take Egypt's incessantly hostile rhetoric seriously. In 1979, President Anwar Sadat warned that Egypt would not passively accept a threat to its water supply. He dramatically declared, "If Ethiopia takes any action to block our right to the Nile water, there will be no alternative but for us to use force." In 2013, President Mohamed Morsi at a televised meeting proclaimed Egypt would support militant forces in Ethiopia and even attack the dam. Over the past seven years, President El-Sisi has warned that tampering with Egypt's Nile water security is its red line, and that the consequences would affect all of the region. Not to appear overly aggressive, El-Sisi has also been speaking with forked tongue that he would prefer diplomacy than not military force, and that Egypt acknowledges the right of Ethiopia to produce power, provided Egypt's water security remains intact. Using Egyptian military power against Ethiopia is not an option. The defeats that Egypt suffered when its forces invaded Ethiopia in the nineteenth century should serve as a lesson not to use military force. In the past, the Egyptian military has launched campaigns to increase Egyptian influence in the Horn of Africa, which includes the Red Sea and the Ethiopian Highlands. History teaches that using military action against Ethiopia will not make Egypt the dominant country or guarantee its exclusive use of Nile waters or solve disputes between the two countries for a lasting peace. The Khedive of Egypt, Ismail Pasha, undertook an invasion of the Ethiopian Empire through military means in the years 1874 and 1876 with the aim of taking control of the whole Nile River Basin to build an empire in Africa. In the Battle of Gundet (1875), Ethiopian forces crushed Egyptian forces. A well-known scholar observed, "Egyptian armies, often with European and American officers, were defeated and practically annihilated by Ethiopian forces led by the Emperor Yohannes on several occasions." In the Battle of Gura (1876), Ethiopian forces routed invading Egyptian forces. One scholar noted, "Gura, fought six months later [Gundet], confirms the superior capabilities of the Ethiopian military." Another noted, "Yohannes met the Egyptians in Hamasien and defeated them decisively at Gura in a three days' battle, 7-9 March 1876." In the Battle of Adwa against colonial Italy which took place on March 1, 1896, Ethiopian wiped out a highly armed modern European army within just a few hours. A highly regarded contemporary historian wrote, "Unlike Napoleon's Russian campaign, the Adwa campaign ended in victory. This is greatness." The historical lesson learned here is that Ethiopia cannot be considered as a country which would bow down to its enernies due to rnilitary superiority. Superior rnilitary equiprnent does not guarantee the achievernent of strategic objectives. The invasions launched by Egypt against Ethiopia in the nineteenth century did not succeed, and in any new war waged against Ethiopia, the result will be the sarne. It is not a stretch of the imagination to compare Israel's wars with Egypt's nineteenth-century campaigns against Ethiopia. During the June 1967 Six-Day War, Egypt was defeated by Israel and its Arab allies. The collapse of the Egyptian army took place in Sinai, and Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula. During the October War of 1973, Egypt won early victories in crossing the Suez Canal and penetrating the defenses of Israel in Sinai. Israel retaliated, crossed the Suez Canal and surrounded Egypt's Third Army. Sinai was finally reclaimed diplomatically by Egypt, after the signing of the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty, when Israel withdrew from Sinai in 1982. The strategic significance and political implications of this war is that it allowed Egypt to reclaim Sinai through diplomacy and the 1979 peace agreement. ln the dispute over the Nile, the lesson for Egypt is that its own history proves the usefulness of shifting frorn rnilitary confrontation to diplornatic resolution. Egypt won back Sinai through diplornacy and a peace agreernent after sorne rnilitary actions. Egypt does not need to be in a continuous state of war with lsrael. Military action against Ethiopia will neither lead to Egyptian domination over the Nile, ensure the safety of Egypt's water supply nor force Ethiopia to become a colonial/client state. Rather than threatening war and attacking Ethiopia, President El-Sisi should give a strong signal to Ethiopia and the Nile Basis countries about peaceful coexistence and prosperity through the fair use of Nile water. lndeed, Egypt should sign the Cornprehensive Frarnework Agreernent which establishes an institutional frarnework to coordinate basin-wide rnanagernent and developrnent of the Nile. The Nile River does not have to be an obstacle between Ethiopia and Egypt; rather, it should become the link between the two nations. Being united by many factors in common such as the history of the river and economics, the two nations should join hands to turn the Nile water into an engine of peace and prosperity. Ethiopia will never be threatened or intimidated militarily by Egypt in its lawful use of the Nile. Certainly, Ethiopia has no intention or desire to threaten or destabilize Egypt or use military means to dictate the way Egypt develops itself. The events involving Gundet and Gura show that Ethiopia will not be intimidated to give up its sovereignty. The events surrounding the Arab-Israeli war show that victory and defeat on the battlefield will not necessarily resolve the political problems involved. The return of Sinai shows the benefit of diplomacy and agreements. A true victory is one that preserves peace and the sovereignty of a nation. The history of Ethiopians indicates that they have always been strong and united in the defense of their homeland. Whether it was the Battle of Gundet and Gura or the Battle of Adwa, the Ethiopian people showed their capability of organizing their troops and using difficult terrains in order to repel their enemies. The defense of Ethiopia against the invasion of Somalia in 1977-1978 gives one more example of the ability of Ethiopian to resist and repel invaders. One lesson that can be learned from these battles is that when the sovereignty of Ethiopia has ever been challenged, then its people have always shown great determination, resilience and ability to defend their land. This glorious tradition is part of every Ethiopian, but the most important lesson that this tradition teaches us is that the greatest victory is that which is won without any battle. But if the battle becomes inevitable, then every Ethiopian is willing to fight for his motherland, making the Ethiopian National Defense Force invincible. What to do? Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan should commit to non-aggression -- pledging not to threaten or use force against one another in violation of the UN Charter, not to support terrorism against each other and to refrain from doing anything that destabilizes the region. The three countries should establish practical arrangements for sharing information, ensuring dam safety, mitigating drought risks, and coordinating reservoir operations. It is important to ensure Ethiopia's rights to manage its water resources fairly and reasonably, while taking into account the concerns of the downstream nations. Technical differences can be sorted out by negotiations and consultations. Moreover, regular military communications and dialogue under the guidance of the African Union should be held and issues addressed in good faith and good will. lf Egypt's clairn is that respect of territorial sovereignty rernoves the possibility of war, then Egypt ought to consider Ethiopia under sirnilar circurnstances. lf Egypt thinks that its security is best guaranteed by peaceful negotiations between itself and lsrael, then Ethiopia rnust be considered under sirnilar conditions. This should not be about Egypt losing or Ethiopia winning; it should be about reaching a solution where neither country is forced to choose between developrnent and security for its neighbor. Egyptian leaders should see the paradox -- the irony-- in rnaking a staternent saying it has no secret plan against lsrael when rnilitary threats are still part of the public discourse about the Ethiopian use of Nile waters. President El-Sisi has articulated a policy that is worth adhering to: Egypt does not need the land of any other country for its security. Ethiopia does not need Egypt to feel insecure in order to develop. The Nile should be rnanaged through cooperation, not coercion; through agreernent, not through threats; and through respect, not through historical anirnosities. This is the peace policy Egypt needs to apply to Ethiopia - and the test to which its rhetoric should be held. Let's join hands and ensure that we all prosper as countries within the Nile Basin and rnake each one of us NlLE GREAT! Read the original article on ENA . ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is positioning itself as an increasingly important investment destination and financial market in Africa, driven by economic reforms and expanding cross-border investment partnerships, Speaker of the House of People's Representatives Ahmed Shide said. Addressing the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO Ethiopia Investor Roadshow, organized by the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX) in collaboration with Dangote Industries Limited in Addis Ababa this afternoon, Ahmed said Ethiopia's economic reforms are opening new opportunities for domestic and international investors. The reforms are also strengthening Africa's capacity to finance its own development, the Speaker elaborated. "With an expanding economy, ongoing reforms, and a growing private sector, we envision Ethiopia becoming an increasingly important investment destination and financial market in Africa." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He highlighted the establishment of the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority, the Ethiopian Securities Exchange and supporting market infrastructure as key milestones in modernizing the country's financial system and mobilizing long-term capital. "Ethiopia's emerging capital market presents significant opportunities for domestic and international investors, financial institutions, and businesses," he said. Ahmed said the introduction of Dangote Petroleum Refinery's initial public offering to qualified Ethiopian investors demonstrates the growing potential for African businesses and investors to engage across national borders. The speaker further stressed that investor confidence, transparency, regulatory cooperation and robust investor protection are essential to building a credible and sustainable capital market, particularly as securities offerings increasingly cross-national borders. He expressed confidence that the country's expanding economy, ongoing reforms and growing private sector would strengthen its position in Africa's investment landscape, welcoming international businesses and financial institutions to participate in the transformation. "We welcome international businesses and financial institutions that wish to participate in this transformation and contribute to the development of our capital market." Addressing the occasion, Dangote Group President Aliko Dangote for his part has reaffirmed his commitment to expanding investments in Ethiopia. "Our investment in Ethiopia has no limit," he said, emphasizing the group's commitment to reinvesting its earnings locally and building a long-term partnership that supports the country's economic transformation. Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter opens with a defining national ambition: building a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state while pursuing sovereign access to the sea. Under the Medemer Government, the government is highly anticipated to translating its electoral mandate into tangible improvements in citizens' lives while strengthening Ethiopia's strategic position in the Horn of Africa. At the heart of this agenda lies Ethiopia's sovereign sea access aspiration. As one of the world's most populous landlocked countries, Ethiopia has a compelling economic interest in reliable access to maritime trade. Securing such access through mutually beneficial arrangements could ease logistical constraints, improve export competitiveness, attract investment and deepen regional economic integration. Yet, maritime access is part of a broader national transformation. The success of Ethiopia's new political chapter will depend equally on consolidating peace, strengthening democratic institutions, advancing national reconciliation and building an inclusive economy. The Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes cooperation, synergy and collective progress, offers a framework for pursuing these priorities. Its credibility will ultimately rest on the government's ability to translate political commitments into measurable results. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ethiopia's domestic progress also carries regional significance. As host of the African Union headquarters and a major political and economic actor in the Horn of Africa, the country has both a strategic interest in regional stability and an opportunity to contribute to it. A stronger Ethiopia, supported by trusted institutions and a resilient economy, would be better positioned to advance its national interests while promoting peace and cooperation across the region. Sovereign Sea Access: A Strategic National Priority For Ethiopia, access to the sea is more than a question of geography. It is closely connected to security, trade, economic competitiveness, national development and long-term strategic interests. Dependence on external maritime corridors exposes the country's economy to transport costs, logistical bottlenecks and disruptions in international trade. Reliable and diversified access to maritime infrastructure could help Ethiopian businesses reach international markets more efficiently, strengthen supply chains and improve the competitiveness of exports. Ethiopia must be an integral part of the Red Sea security architecture. As a major regional actor with longstanding contributions to peacekeeping under the United Nations and peace and security efforts across the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia has a compelling strategic interest in the security of this vital maritime corridor and a meaningful contribution to make. Excluding a country of Ethiopia's regional significance from decisions affecting Red Sea security would leave a critical stakeholder outside a process with direct implications for its economic and national interests. Ethiopia should therefore have a meaningful seat at the table, enabling it to contribute to maritime security, protect international shipping, strengthen regional stability and help safeguard one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Ultimately, the measure of progress will be whether Ethiopia can expand its maritime options, reduce trade constraints and strengthen its economic resilience while contributing to stability across the Horn of Africa. National Unity as Foundation of Strategic Ambition No national ambition can be sustained without internal stability and a shared sense of purpose. Ethiopia's new political chapter must therefore begin with the responsibility to strengthen national unity, address longstanding grievances and rebuild public confidence. The country's cultural diversity, complex history and competing political interests make inclusive state building essential. Unity cannot be achieved through declarations alone. It requires equal citizenship, constitutional protection, fair access to opportunities and institutions capable of managing disagreements peacefully. The Medemer approach can help create common ground among political parties, government institutions, civil society organizations, religious institutions, traditional leaders and communities. The national dialogue process offers an opportunity to address historical grievances, identify shared interests and build a stronger foundation for consensus. For this process to succeed, participation must be meaningful, diverse perspectives must be heard, and recommendations must inform practical reforms. National reconciliation should not be reduced to a political slogan; it must produce greater trust, improved relations among communities and more effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. Democratic Institutions: Turning the Mandate into Public Trust The durability of Ethiopia's political transition will depend heavily on the performance of its democratic institutions. Parliament, the judiciary, electoral bodies and executive institutions must operate within their constitutional mandates and provide effective mechanisms for accountability. The House of Peoples' Representatives has a responsibility not only to enact legislation but also to scrutinize government performance, examine public expenditure and ensure that national policies respond to citizens' needs. Effective parliamentary oversight can help identify implementation gaps, improve public spending and strengthen accountability. An independent and accessible judiciary is equally important. Citizens must be able to seek remedies when their rights are violated, while disputes should be resolved through impartial legal procedures. Consistent application of the law would reinforce equal protection and improve confidence in public institutions. Political parties also have a responsibility to strengthen democratic practices by presenting credible policy alternatives, engaging in constructive debate and respecting constitutional procedures. The government, in turn, must protect lawful political participation, civic engagement and public criticism. Combating corruption, reducing administrative inefficiency and improving public services are equally important. Transparent procurement, responsible financial management and accessible complaint mechanisms would help ensure that public resources serve their intended purposes. These reforms are directly connected to Ethiopia's broader strategic ambitions. Predictable institutions and accountable governance can strengthen investor confidence, improve the business environment and support the effective implementation of infrastructure and development projects. A government that earns public trust at home is also better positioned to build credible partnerships abroad. Democratic accountability is therefore not separate from national strategy; it is one of the foundations on which sustainable national progress depends. Economic Transformation and Building the Capacity for Sovereignty Ethiopia's pursuit of sea access must be supported by an economy capable of turning improved connectivity into prosperity. Access to ports and international markets can create opportunities, but the benefits will depend on domestic productivity, competitive industries and the capacity to generate value. In this regard, Ethiopia's "Made in Ethiopia" industrial movement is playing an important role in strengthening domestic production, advancing import substitution and expanding the country's manufacturing capacity. By encouraging local industries to produce goods previously sourced from abroad, the initiative supports economic self-reliance, reduces import dependence and creates opportunities for domestic investment and job creation. Agriculture remains central to Ethiopia's food security and economy. Under the Medemer philosophy, the country has made notable progress, particularly in wheat production. Expanding irrigation, mechanization, research and agro-processing can further boost productivity, reduce climate vulnerability and increase farmers' incomes. Industrialization, manufacturing and digital transformation are equally vital to diversifying exports, creating jobs and strengthening domestic production. Reliable power, efficient logistics, access to finance and a skilled workforce will be essential to building competitive businesses. Improved maritime connectivity could lower trade barriers and connect Ethiopian producers to global markets, while stronger domestic industries would help the country capture greater value from international trade. Horn of Africa and Red Sea Region Cooperation for Shared Prosperity Ethiopia's national future is closely connected to developments across the Horn of Africa. Conflict, displacement, food insecurity and climate pressures frequently cross borders, while political tensions can disrupt trade and threaten the livelihoods of border communities. The pursuit of sea access must therefore be approached within a wider framework of regional cooperation. Ethiopia's strategic and economic interests must be connected to the Red Sea coast in the near future for mutual benefits. Port operations, transport corridors, logistics services and cross-border infrastructure can create commercial opportunities for participating countries. Improved connectivity can strengthen regional supply chains, expand markets and encourage investment in transport, manufacturing and trade-related services. A more stable and connected Horn of Africa would benefit Ethiopia's maritime aspirations while supporting the development priorities of its neighbors. Ethiopia's regional influence will therefore depend not only on the scale of its ambitions but also on its ability to build trust, sustain dialogue and demonstrate that cooperation can deliver tangible benefits. Climate Resilience and Water Security on Nile River Equally important to Ethiopia's ambition for sovereign sea access, the new Medemer Government must maximize the development potential of the Abay (Blue Nile) River by advancing additional hydropower and irrigation projects. Harnessing this strategic resource is vital to expanding electricity generation, strengthening food security and accelerating economic transformation. Climate resilience remains central to this ambition. Droughts, floods and shifting rainfall patterns threaten agriculture, water supplies, infrastructure and livelihoods across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia's investment in hydropower and irrigation must therefore go hand in hand with sustainable water management, environmental protection and climate adaptation. For Ethiopia, maximizing the Abay River's potential is not merely an energy or irrigation priority; it is a strategic pillar of economic sovereignty, food security and long-term national development. Youth and Women: Expanding the Foundations of National Progress Ethiopia's young population represents a major opportunity for economic growth, innovation and national renewal. Realizing this potential requires more than expanding education; it demands relevant skills, productive employment, entrepreneurship and meaningful participation in public life. Limited employment opportunities can deepen frustration, particularly when young people feel excluded from decisions affecting their future. Investment in technical and vocational education, digital skills and employment-intensive sectors would help connect education with the needs of the economy. Stronger links between schools, universities, training institutions and employers could improve the transition from education to employment. Support for entrepreneurship and small businesses could also enable young people to turn their skills and ideas into productive economic activity. Youth participation is equally important in national reconciliation, community development and public debate. Providing meaningful opportunities for young people to contribute to public affairs would strengthen social cohesion and ensure that national policies respond to their priorities. Women's participation is another essential component of inclusive development. Expanding access to education, employment, finance, public services and leadership would allow more citizens to contribute to national progress and strengthen household welfare. These investments have strategic significance. A skilled, productive and economically empowered population would strengthen domestic industries, improve export competitiveness and help Ethiopia benefit from expanded regional and international trade. National ambition becomes more sustainable when citizens have a genuine stake in its realization. Empowering young people and women is therefore not simply a social objective; it is an investment in Ethiopia's productive capacity, stability and long-term prosperity. From National Ambition to Measurable Results The credibility of Ethiopia's new political chapter will ultimately depend on implementation. The government must translate its priorities into clear targets, allocate resources according to national needs and establish mechanisms for assessing progress. Security, employment, public service delivery, institutional accountability and economic resilience should be central measures of performance. Federal and regional authorities must coordinate their responsibilities while respecting constitutional mandates and local circumstances. Consultation with communities, businesses, professional associations and civil society can improve decision-making and help identify emerging problems. Efficient public financial management, stronger procurement systems and effective anti-corruption measures would help ensure that limited resources deliver meaningful results. The government must also balance long-term infrastructure investments with immediate public needs. Citizens expect improved access to health care, education, affordable food, employment and personal security. Progress in these areas will shape public confidence in the administration. Strategic ambitions and domestic responsibilities should reinforce each other. Maritime access can expand economic opportunities and its full value should depend on productive industries, capable institutions, skilled workers and a stable political environment. The ultimate test is whether national policies improve the lives of citizens while strengthening Ethiopia's ability to pursue its interests through peaceful and constructive engagement. All in all, Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter presents an opportunity to strengthen the foundations of a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state. Its success will depend on the government's ability to translate its electoral mandate and the Medemer philosophy into tangible progress in national unity, security, institutional accountability and living standards. At the heart of the country's strategic ambition is sovereign access to the sea. Pursued through mutually beneficial arrangements, maritime connectivity could help ease trade constraints, strengthen export competitiveness and deepen regional economic integration as well as ensure lasting peace. Beyond its borders, Ethiopia must strengthen constructive relations with neighboring states, advance cooperation on trade, infrastructure, energy and climate resilience, and support regional efforts to prevent conflict. Its engagement with the African Union and IGAD can help advance these goals when backed by consistent diplomacy and practical commitments. The government's responsibility is therefore both national and regional: to build a state that citizens trust, an economy that expands opportunities and a foreign policy that advances national interests while respecting the legitimate interests of others. Sovereign access to the sea may be at the heart of Ethiopia's national ambition, but national unity, democratic governance and economic transformation will determine its success. The defining measure of the Medemer State will be its ability to turn this ambition into lasting improvements in citizens' lives while contributing to a more peaceful, stable and economically integrated Horn of Africa. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is seeking increased investment and stronger public-private partnerships to expand renewable energy use and support agricultural productivity, business growth and improved livelihoods. The ongoing Second Ethiopian Renewable Energy Summit 2026 which opened today focuses on attracting investment, expanding energy access and strengthening the contribution of renewable energy to the country's economic development. Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Iteffa, through his representative, noted that electric power is essential for economic transformation, industrial development, public services, agricultural productivity and improved living standards. Therefore, Ethiopia needs to expand its national grid while complementing it with decentralized renewable energy solutions, including solar home systems, mini-grids and technologies that enable businesses and communities to use energy productively. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "Our objective must be to move from dialogue to investments, from isolated initiatives to scale-up solutions, and from commitments to implementation," he said. The Minister also underscored the importance of private-sector participation in the energy transition through capital investment, technical expertise, innovation, distribution networks, job creation and local manufacturing. He said expanding the market requires a predictable policy and regulatory environment, access to finance and foreign exchange, quality standards and business models that make renewable energy solutions affordable and sustainable. Agriculture Minister Addisu Arega, through his representative, highlighted the role of renewable energy in improving agricultural production, addressing climate-related challenges and strengthening farmers' resilience to irregular rainfall and rising production costs. He said solar-powered irrigation can improve farmers' access to water, reduce dependence on diesel-powered pumps and support crop diversification. Renewable energy can also power cold storage, refrigerated transport and other facilities that help preserve agricultural products and reduce post-harvest losses. Moreover, renewable energy can support agricultural processing, dairy production, rural water supply, veterinary services, digital agriculture and access to agricultural inputs. However, high upfront costs, limited access to affordable finance, gaps in technical skills and challenges in equipment maintenance remain barriers to wider adoption. Addisu emphasized the need for stronger public-private partnerships, technical training, affordable financing and coordinated planning across the agriculture, water and energy sectors to ensure that renewable energy technologies meet the needs of farmers and rural communities. For her part, Ethiopian Solar Energy Development Association (ESEDA) General Manager Yemissirach Sisay said the summit seeks to demonstrate the readiness and capacity of private companies to contribute to Ethiopia's energy transition and turn the country's renewable energy potential into practical results. "The private sector is not waiting on the sidelines of national development," she noted. The General Manager highlighted opportunities in solar-powered water pumps for smallholder farmers, mini-grids for communities without adequate electricity access, clean cooking technologies and sustainable electric mobility. Addressing investment risks, foreign exchange constraints, taxation and financing challenges would help local companies expand from small-scale distribution to larger renewable energy projects. Yemissirach also stressed the importance of cooperation among African renewable energy associations to share experience, improve regulatory coordination, expand regional trade and support the development of a more integrated African energy market. The summit has brought together representatives of the government, renewable energy companies, private-sector investors, financial institutions, development partners and other stakeholders The summit, which runs up to 17 October 2026, provides a platform for collaboration and investment in the renewable energy sector.
